findings.message: Repo Scout — GitHub API scraper for cybersecurity education repos

meta.notes: Build the primary GitHub scraper using the GitHub Search API. Search strategies: (1) Topic-based search — query repos tagged with: cybersecurity, ethical-hacking, infosec, penetration-testing, ctf, network-security, cloud-security, malware-analysis, digital-forensics, incident-response, oscp, ceh, comptia, security-plus, ccna, sysadmin, linux-administration, windows-server. (2) Keyword search — search repo names and descriptions for: 'course', 'curriculum', 'slides', 'lecture', 'lab', 'workshop', 'bootcamp', 'training', 'educational', 'learning-path', 'study-guide', 'certification', 'exam-prep'. (3) Awesome-list mining — scrape awesome-cybersecurity, awesome-hacking, awesome-pentest, awesome-security, awesome-infosec and similar curated lists for linked repos. (4) Organization scanning — scan known edu orgs: OWASP, SANS, NIST repos, university CS departments with public course materials. (5) User-based — find prolific cybersecurity educators on GitHub and scan their repos. Filters: minimum 10 stars, has license file, last updated within 2 years, contains markdown/HTML/PDF/PPTX content (not just code tools). Output: per-repo JSON record with metadata, content preview, and Hexworth house recommendation. CLI: node _tools/repo-scout/scout.js scan --topic cybersecurity --min-stars 10.

findings.message: Repo Scout — GitLab and alternative platform scrapers

meta.notes: Extend Repo Scout beyond GitHub to other platforms. GitLab: use GitLab API (v4) to search public projects with cybersecurity/education topics. Many university courses host on GitLab (self-hosted instances and gitlab.com). Bitbucket: search public repos — less common for edu content but some exist. SourceHut: niche but growing, some security research hosted here. Academic sources: (1) MIT OpenCourseWare — scrape course listings for computer science and cybersecurity, find linked GitHub repos or downloadable materials. (2) Coursera/edX — identify open-source companion repos for security courses. (3) Open Textbook Library — search for CC-licensed cybersecurity and networking textbooks. (4) Archive.org — search for archived educational materials with permissive licenses. Non-repo content sources: (5) SlideShare/SpeakerDeck — scrape for cybersecurity presentation decks with CC licenses. (6) NIST/CISA public resources — training materials, frameworks, guides (all public domain). Each platform gets its own scraper module under _tools/repo-scout/scrapers/. Common output format so all discoveries feed into the same manifest.

findings.message: Repo Scout — Content classifier and house mapper

meta.notes: Build an automated classifier that analyzes discovered repos and maps them to Hexworth houses. Analysis steps: (1) File type inventory — count markdown, HTML, PPTX, PDF, Jupyter notebooks, YAML, code files to determine content type (lecture slides, labs, reference docs, tools). (2) Keyword extraction — scan README and top-level docs for domain keywords: map to houses using keyword → house lookup table (e.g., 'firewall' → shield/web, 'malware' → dark-arts, 'AWS' → cloud, 'subnet' → web, 'Arduino' → forge, 'Python' → code, 'cryptography' → key, 'SIEM' → eye, 'PowerShell' → script). (3) License classifier — categorize license permissiveness (Public Domain > CC0 > MIT > Apache 2.0 > CC-BY > CC-BY-SA > GPL > CC-BY-NC > proprietary/unknown). Flag non-commercial licenses as 'review required'. (4) Quality scoring — composite score based on: stars, forks, recency, content volume, file organization, README quality, license permissiveness. (5) Conversion effort estimator — small (< 10 files, simple markdown), medium (10-50 files, mixed formats), large (50+ files or complex PPTX/PDF conversion). Output: enriched discovery record with house[], contentType, license, qualityScore, conversionEffort, recommended priority. CLI: node _tools/repo-scout/scout.js classify --input discoveries.json.

findings.message: Repo Scout — Discovery dashboard and review workflow

meta.notes: Build a dashboard to review, approve, and track discovered repos. Features: (1) Discovery browser — filterable/sortable table of all discovered repos: name, URL, house mapping, quality score, license, conversion effort, status (new/reviewed/approved/forked/converting/converted/rejected). (2) Review workflow — click a discovery to see full details: README preview, file tree, content samples, license text, similar repos already in pipeline. Mark as 'approve for fork', 'reject' (with reason), or 'bookmark for later'. (3) Fork tracker — once approved, track the fork process: forked → content extracted → conversion sprint created → conversion in progress → integrated into Prime. (4) Stats dashboard — total discoveries, by house, by license, by status, conversion pipeline metrics. (5) Scheduled scanning — configure cron/scheduled task to run scrapers weekly and surface new discoveries. (6) Duplicate detection — flag repos that contain substantially similar content to already-forked repos or existing Prime content. Build as HTML page in _tools/repo-scout/dashboard.html or as CLI reports: node _tools/repo-scout/scout.js dashboard, node _tools/repo-scout/scout.js report --format md.

findings.message: Repo Scout — Auto-fork and content extraction pipeline

meta.notes: Automate the fork → extract → stage pipeline. Auto-fork: use GitHub API (or gh CLI) to fork approved repos to the FM-256 GitHub organization. Naming convention: hexworth-source-{original-repo-name}. Content extraction: (1) Clone the forked repo locally to _planning/repo-scout-imports/{repo-name}/. (2) Extract convertible content — PPTX files (use python-pptx to extract text + images), PDF files (extract text with PyMuPDF/pdfplumber), Markdown files (copy directly), Jupyter notebooks (extract cells), HTML slides (copy directly). (3) Generate a conversion manifest: source file → target Prime file mapping, with house assignment and module numbering. (4) Auto-create sprint items — for each repo, generate EHE-style sprint items in sprints.json for the conversion work (one item per module/chapter). Safeguards: never auto-fork without approval flag, never overwrite existing Prime content, always preserve attribution and license in extracted content. CLI: node _tools/repo-scout/scout.js fork RS-{id}, node _tools/repo-scout/scout.js extract {repo-name}.

findings.message: Repo Scout — License compliance and attribution tracker

meta.notes: Build a license compliance system to ensure all forked and converted content respects original licenses. Components: (1) License database — for every forked repo, store: original license text, license type (SPDX identifier), original author(s), original URL, fork date, any license conditions (attribution required, share-alike, non-commercial). (2) Attribution generator — automatically generate attribution notices for converted content. Each Prime module converted from external source gets a footer or metadata field: 'Adapted from [Original Title] by [Author], licensed under [License]. Original: [URL]'. (3) License compatibility matrix — which licenses allow what: can we modify? must we share-alike? can we use commercially? must we attribute? (4) Compliance checker — scan _planning/repo-scout-imports/ and cross-reference with license database, flag any content lacking license info or using incompatible licenses. (5) NOTICE file — maintain a master NOTICE.md listing all third-party content sources, licenses, and attribution. This is non-negotiable — protects Hexworth legally and respects open-source community. Store at _tools/repo-scout/licenses.json and generate NOTICE.md.

findings.message: Repo Scout — Conversion template engine for common formats

meta.notes: Build reusable conversion templates to speed up the raw-to-Prime pipeline. Templates needed: (1) PPTX → Presentation HTML — extract slides from PowerPoint, convert to Prime slide-based presentation format with correct house theme (auto-detect house from RS-4 classification). Handle: text extraction, bullet points, images (export to assets/), tables, code blocks, speaker notes. (2) Markdown → Presentation HTML — convert structured markdown (headings = slides) to Prime presentation format. (3) PDF → Presentation HTML — extract pages/sections, OCR if scanned, convert to slides. (4) Jupyter Notebook → Lab HTML — convert notebook cells to Prime interactive lab format. (5) Quiz/Test Bank → Quiz HTML — parse common test bank formats (CSV, QTI, Respondus, plain text Q&A) into Prime quiz format. Each template: auto-applies correct house color palette, adds Hexworth navigation chrome, generates content-registry.js entry stub, creates progress tracking hooks. CLI: node _tools/repo-scout/convert.js --input source.pptx --house dark-arts --module-id ehe-01 --type presentation. This is the force multiplier — makes bulk conversion feasible instead of hand-building every module.

findings.message: Repo Scout — Initial seed scan and first batch fork

meta.notes: Run the first production scan and fork the initial batch of high-value repos. Target: 50-100 discovered repos, fork top 10-20 highest-quality finds. Priority search targets by house: Dark Arts (ethical hacking courses, CTF writeup collections, pentest methodology repos), Web (networking courses, CCNA/Network+ study materials, protocol labs), Cloud (AWS/Azure/GCP security courses, cloud architecture materials), Code (programming courses with security focus, algorithm visualizations), Shield (GRC frameworks, compliance guides, risk assessment templates), Key (cryptography courses, crypto challenge sets), Eye (SIEM/SOC training materials, log analysis courses, threat hunting playbooks), Script (automation courses, scripting tutorials, DevOps security), Forge (hardware hacking, IoT security, embedded systems courses). Deliverable: first discoveries.json populated, first batch of forks completed, conversion sprints auto-generated for top 5 repos. This proves the pipeline end-to-end and starts feeding fresh content into the conversion queue.

findings.message: Neon Server — Hardware inventory, drive assessment, and BIOS/UEFI setup

meta.notes: Physical setup and inventory of the Neon main server. Tasks: (1) Document hardware specs — CPU, RAM (total and configuration), motherboard model, NIC(s), GPU if any, PSU wattage. (2) Inventory all hard drives — make, model, capacity, interface (SATA, NVMe, SAS), current health (SMART data), RPM/type (HDD vs SSD). (3) Decide drive layout strategy: which drive(s) for OS, which for data/databases, which for backups, any hot spares. (4) BIOS/UEFI configuration — boot order, enable virtualization (VT-x/AMD-V, VT-d/IOMMU if needed), AHCI mode for SATA, NVMe configuration, fan/thermal settings, wake-on-LAN if desired. (5) Check/update firmware — BIOS, drive firmware, NIC firmware, RAID controller firmware if applicable. (6) Physical setup — rack/shelf placement, power connections (UPS if available), network cabling (at least 1 Gbps, ideally 2.5/10G if hardware supports), KVM or remote management (IPMI/iLO/iDRAC if server-grade). Deliverable: hardware manifest document and drive layout plan approved before OS install.

findings.message: Neon Server — OS installation and base system configuration

meta.notes: Install and configure the base operating system on Neon. Decisions: (1) OS selection — Ubuntu Server 24.04 LTS (stable, wide support, 5-year maintenance), Debian 12 (rock-solid, minimal), Rocky Linux 9 / AlmaLinux 9 (RHEL-based, enterprise), or Proxmox VE (if running VMs/containers as primary workload). (2) Disk partitioning — recommended layout: boot partition (1GB, ext4), root partition (50-100GB SSD, ext4/xfs), swap (1-2x RAM or 8GB cap), /home (SSD, user data), /var (separate partition for logs/databases, SSD), /data (large HDD pool for bulk storage — mounted separately). Consider LVM for flexible resizing. (3) RAID configuration — if multiple drives: RAID 1 for OS (mirror for redundancy), RAID 5/6 or ZFS raidz1/raidz2 for data pool (capacity with parity), or ZFS mirror pairs. ZFS preferred if RAM allows (1GB per TB of storage). (4) Base config — hostname (neon), static IP on LAN, SSH server (key-only auth, disable password auth, non-standard port optional), firewall (ufw or firewalld — deny all, allow SSH), timezone, NTP sync, automatic security updates (unattended-upgrades). (5) User setup — admin user, sudo group, SSH key deployment from dev machines.

findings.message: Neon Server — Storage pool setup and mount strategy

meta.notes: Configure storage pools and mount points for organized data management. Tasks: (1) Create storage pools — if using ZFS: create zpools (tank, fast-pool for SSDs, bulk-pool for HDDs), set compression (lz4), set atime=off, create datasets for each purpose. If using LVM: create volume groups and logical volumes. If using mdadm RAID: create arrays, format, mount. (2) Mount point structure: /data/hexworth/ (Hexworth project repos and working copies), /data/databases/ (database data directories), /data/backups/ (automated backup target), /data/media/ (raw source content — PPTX, PDF, videos), /data/repos/ (forked GitHub repos from Repo Scout), /data/scratch/ (temp workspace for conversions). (3) Permissions — create hexworth group, set proper ownership and permissions on each mount point, ACLs if needed for multi-user access. (4) fstab entries — ensure all mounts persist across reboots with correct options (noatime, nofail for non-critical). (5) Monitoring — set up disk space alerts (df thresholds), SMART monitoring (smartmontools + smartd for drive health alerts), ZFS scrub schedule if using ZFS (monthly). (6) Network shares — Samba share for Windows access from dev machines, NFS for Linux clients, or both. Ensure Hexworth project data is accessible from the WSL development environment.

findings.message: Neon Server — Database server installation (PostgreSQL + MongoDB)

meta.notes: Install and configure database servers on Neon. PostgreSQL (relational): (1) Install PostgreSQL 16 (latest stable). (2) Configure postgresql.conf — listen_addresses (LAN IP or 0.0.0.0), port 5432, shared_buffers (25% of RAM), effective_cache_size (75% of RAM), work_mem, maintenance_work_mem, WAL settings for durability. (3) Configure pg_hba.conf — local auth (peer/md5), LAN access (md5/scram-sha-256, restrict to subnet). (4) Create databases: hexworth_prime (Prime platform data), hexworth_arena (Arena game data), hexworth_colosseum (Colosseum game data), hexworth_analytics (usage analytics, progress tracking). (5) Create application user(s) with least-privilege roles. MongoDB (document store): (1) Install MongoDB 7.x Community. (2) Configure mongod.conf — bindIp (LAN), port 27017, storage.dbPath (/data/databases/mongodb), enable authentication. (3) Create databases: hexworth_content (content registry, course materials), hexworth_users (user profiles, progress). (4) Create application users with appropriate roles. Both: (5) Firewall rules — allow DB ports only from trusted LAN IPs. (6) Verify connectivity from dev machines. (7) Basic backup scripts (pg_dump, mongodump) running on cron to /data/backups/.

findings.message: Neon Server — Network configuration and remote access

meta.notes: Configure Neon's network for reliable LAN access and optional remote access. LAN setup: (1) Static IP assignment — either static in netplan/NetworkManager or DHCP reservation on router. (2) Hostname resolution — add neon to /etc/hosts on dev machines, or set up local DNS (Pi-hole, dnsmasq) so 'neon' or 'neon.local' resolves from all devices. (3) mDNS/Avahi — install avahi-daemon so neon.local works via mDNS (zero-config). (4) Firewall rules — allow: SSH (22 or custom), PostgreSQL (5432), MongoDB (27017), Samba (445), NFS (2049), HTTP/HTTPS (80/443 for future web services), monitoring (9090 Prometheus, 3000 Grafana). Deny all else. Remote access (optional): (5) Tailscale or WireGuard VPN — secure tunnel for accessing Neon from outside LAN without exposing ports to internet. Tailscale is zero-config; WireGuard is lighter but manual. (6) SSH jump host — if no VPN, SSH on non-standard port with fail2ban for brute-force protection. (7) Dynamic DNS — if ISP gives dynamic IP, set up DDNS (DuckDNS, Cloudflare, No-IP) for consistent remote hostname. (8) Speed test — verify network throughput between dev machines and Neon (iperf3).

findings.message: Neon Server — Docker and container runtime setup

meta.notes: Install Docker and container infrastructure on Neon for running services. Tasks: (1) Install Docker Engine (not Docker Desktop — server has no GUI). Add docker group, add admin user to docker group. (2) Install Docker Compose v2 (plugin). (3) Configure Docker — data-root on data drive (not OS drive), default logging driver (json-file with max-size/max-file rotation), DNS settings, default network. (4) Set up docker-compose project structure: /data/hexworth/docker/ with per-service compose files. (5) Initial containers to consider: Portainer (web UI for managing containers), Nginx Proxy Manager or Traefik (reverse proxy for web services), Watchtower (auto-update containers), Uptime Kuma (service monitoring). (6) Container networking — create hexworth-net bridge network for inter-container communication. (7) Volume strategy — named volumes stored on data drives, bind mounts for config files. (8) If databases end up containerized instead of bare-metal (NE-4), set up persistent volumes on data drives with proper backup hooks. Docker gives flexibility to spin up dev/staging environments, run Repo Scout scrapers in containers, or add services like Redis, Elasticsearch, or MinIO later without cluttering the base OS.

findings.message: Neon Server — Backup strategy and disaster recovery

meta.notes: Set up automated backups and a disaster recovery plan. Backup targets: (1) Databases — pg_dump (PostgreSQL) and mongodump (MongoDB) nightly to /data/backups/db/ with 7-day rotation. (2) Configuration — /etc/ configs, Docker compose files, cron jobs, firewall rules — backed up weekly. (3) Hexworth project data — git repos are self-backed-up to GitHub, but local working copies and non-git data (raw source content, converted assets, uploaded media) need backup. (4) Backup destination — local backup drive (separate physical drive from data drives), plus off-site: rsync to a cloud storage bucket (Backblaze B2 is cheapest at $5/TB/month), or rsync to a second machine. Tools: (5) restic or borg for deduplicated, encrypted, incremental backups. (6) Cron schedule: databases nightly, full system weekly, configs on change. (7) Backup verification — monthly test restore to confirm backups are valid (untested backups are not backups). (8) Disaster recovery runbook — document: how to rebuild Neon from scratch, where backups live, restore order (OS → storage → databases → services → data), estimated recovery time. Store runbook in the repo, not only on Neon.

findings.message: Neon Server — Monitoring, alerting, and health dashboard

meta.notes: Set up monitoring so you know when something goes wrong before it becomes a problem. Stack: (1) Prometheus (metrics collection) — node_exporter for system metrics (CPU, RAM, disk, network, temperature), postgres_exporter for PostgreSQL metrics, mongodb_exporter for MongoDB metrics. (2) Grafana (dashboards) — system overview dashboard (CPU, RAM, disk I/O, network throughput, temperatures), database dashboard (connections, query performance, cache hit ratio, replication lag), Docker dashboard (container status, resource usage), storage dashboard (pool usage, SMART health, ZFS scrub status). (3) Alerting — Grafana alerts or Alertmanager: disk space > 85%, CPU sustained > 90%, RAM > 90%, drive SMART warning, database connection failures, backup job failures, container crash/restart. Notification channels: email, Slack/Discord webhook, or Pushover for mobile push. (4) Uptime Kuma — simple uptime monitor for all services (HTTP endpoints, TCP ports, Docker containers), public status page optional. (5) Log aggregation (optional) — Loki + Promtail for centralized log searching, or simple logrotate + journald for basics. All monitoring services run as Docker containers (NE-6).

findings.message: Neon Server — Security hardening and access control

meta.notes: Harden Neon against attack — practice what Hexworth teaches. SSH hardening: (1) Key-only authentication (disable PasswordAuthentication), (2) disable root login, (3) AllowUsers whitelist, (4) fail2ban for brute-force protection (ban after 5 failed attempts, 1-hour ban). Firewall: (5) ufw/firewalld — default deny incoming, explicit allow per service, rate-limit SSH. System hardening: (6) Automatic security updates (unattended-upgrades on Ubuntu/Debian, dnf-automatic on RHEL-based). (7) Remove unnecessary services (telnet, FTP, avahi if not needed). (8) Disable unused network protocols (IPv6 if not used). (9) File integrity monitoring — AIDE or Tripwire for detecting unauthorized changes to system files. (10) AppArmor or SELinux — enforce mandatory access controls. (11) Kernel hardening — sysctl settings (disable IP forwarding unless routing, enable SYN cookies, disable ICMP redirects). (12) User audit — review /etc/passwd, no shared accounts, strong passwords for any non-key accounts. (13) Regular vulnerability scanning — run Lynis audit monthly, review findings. (14) Logging — ensure auditd is running for security event logging, forward logs to centralized location. This is Hexworth's own server — it should be a model of the security practices we teach.

findings.message: Neon Server — Dev environment integration and workflow connection

meta.notes: Connect Neon to the daily development workflow so it's actually used, not forgotten. Dev machine integration: (1) Mount Neon shares on WSL — Samba mount in /etc/fstab or systemd automount so /mnt/neon/hexworth is always available. (2) Database connection profiles — set up .pgpass and mongosh connection strings on dev machines for quick DB access. (3) VS Code Remote-SSH — configure VS Code to connect to Neon for editing files directly on server when needed. (4) Git workflow — option A: continue developing locally, push to GitHub, Neon pulls from GitHub (webhook or cron). Option B: develop on Neon via SSH/Remote, push to GitHub from Neon. Option C: local dev + Neon as CI/staging (git push triggers Neon deploy). (5) Repo Scout integration — configure _tools/repo-scout to write discoveries to Neon's database instead of local JSON. (6) Content pipeline — raw source content (PPTX, PDF from EHE, forked repos) stored on Neon's bulk storage, accessed from dev machines via network share. (7) Firebase sync — option to run Firebase CLI from Neon for deployments (firebase deploy from server). (8) Alias/shortcut setup — add ssh aliases and shell functions to .bashrc on dev machines for quick Neon access (ssh neon, neon-db, neon-logs).

findings.message: Explore Multiplayer Mode for The Hive

meta.notes: Explore and design multiplayer capabilities for The Hive dungeon crawler. Currently single-player only (solo room navigation, puzzles, Red Queen AI). Multiplayer concepts to explore: (1) Co-op Exploration — 2-4 players navigate the facility together in real-time via Firestore, see each other's positions on the SVG map, collaborate on puzzles, split up to cover more ground. (2) Competitive Speedrun — players race through the same floor simultaneously, first to solve all puzzles wins, ghost positions visible on map. (3) Asymmetric Mode — one player controls the Red Queen (sets traps, locks doors, chooses dialogue) while others explore, turning PvE into PvP. (4) Party System — lobby/invite system, shared session codes, voice/text chat integration. (5) Cooperative Puzzles — puzzles that require multiple players to solve simultaneously (one player sees clues the other needs). Technical: Firestore real-time listeners for player positions and game state, session documents with player roster, conflict resolution for shared puzzle state, latency handling for room transitions. Current architecture: HiveEngine.js manages state, MapRenderer.js draws SVG, RoomRenderer.js handles UI — would need multiplayer state layer on top. Ties into F-23 (messaging) and F-21 (profiles) for player identity.

findings.message: AI Art Pipeline — FAL-Generated Game Assets (Debugger Pilot)

meta.notes: Establish a FAL (fal.ai) image generation pipeline to produce high-quality game art assets, replacing hand-coded canvas pixel art. Pilot game: shield-debugger.applet.html (F-44 Doom-style FPS) — chosen because raycasting engines live or die by texture quality and enemy sprite variety. PHASE 1 — DEBUGGER PILOT ASSETS: (1) Wall textures — 64x64 or 128x128 tileable textures for each system layer: Userspace (clean server room tiles, fluorescent lighting), Network Stack (cable conduit walls, blinking LEDs), Kernel (raw circuit board traces, capacitor arrays), Firmware (dark metallic plating, warning stripes). Need floor/ceiling textures too. (2) Enemy sprites — each enemy type needs front-facing sprite at minimum, ideally 4-8 angle views for raycasting rotation: Buffer Overflow (bloated glitching mass), Trojan (disguised friendly process + revealed hostile form), Worm (segmented snake-like, multiply animation), Ransomware (padlock-headed enforcer), Zero-Day (glitch/stealth shimmer). Death/pain animation frames for each. (3) Weapon sprites — first-person view-model sprites for each weapon: Firewall Shotgun, Antivirus Rifle, Packet Sniffer Scanner, Sandbox Grenade, IDS Turret, Full Format BFG. Need idle + fire + reload frames. (4) HUD elements — health bar frame, ammo counter, minimap border, threat scanner overlay, pickup item sprites (ammo boxes, health kits = system patches, armor = encryption). (5) Title screen and level transition art. PHASE 2 — PIPELINE STANDARDIZATION: Once Debugger pilot proves the workflow, document the FAL prompt templates, asset size conventions, and color palette rules. Apply pipeline to other games: Root Access (F-45) tile sprites, Runner games (F-42) character/chaser sprites, Flapper games (F-43) obstacle and environment art. TECHNICAL NOTES: FAL supports FLUX, Stable Diffusion, and other models. For pixel art / game sprites, use img2img with pixel art LoRAs or style prompts. Output as PNG sprite sheets, slice into individual frames. Store generated assets in _app/assets/generated/ with source prompts documented. Canvas games load via Image() objects — no build step needed. Consider generating at 2x resolution and downscaling for crisp pixel-perfect rendering on retina displays. SESSION 2026-02-27: Pipeline proven with generate_trophy_medals.py script. Generated 4 trophy/medal icons, 11 FEH module icons, 18 vault module icons, 1 matrix house icon = 34 assets total via fal.ai FLUX.1 [dev].

findings.message: Colosseum Multiplayer — Co-op Sync Engine

meta.notes: Build hexworth-coop-sync.js (~300 lines). createSession() writes run doc + joinCode index. joinSession() looks up code, adds player, subscribes. subscribeToState() via onSnapshot. submitActionAtomically() via Firestore transaction with optimistic lock on round number. Per-player hands in players/{uid} subcollection. broadcastActivity() writes to events subcollection.

findings.message: Colosseum Multiplayer — Lobby Host/Join Flow

meta.notes: Expand lobby.js to branch local vs multiplayer. Host path: call createSession(), display room code, show player list from Firestore snapshot. Join path: replace error message with joinSession(code), subscribe to player list. Host-only Start Game button. Role selection synced — both players see picks in real time.

findings.message: Colosseum Multiplayer — Board Real-Time Sync

meta.notes: Modify board.js to branch local vs multiplayer on load/save. Multiplayer: subscribeToState() drives renderBoard(). Action confirm calls submitActionAtomically() instead of local resolveRound(). Handle per-player hand from subcollection. Timer runs locally but skip-round still applies server-side. Resolution sequence plays on both clients from shared state update.

findings.message: Aminos Bot — Script House Specialist (Linux Tutor)

meta.notes: Specialist bot for Script House. Train on Linux Mastery modules, bash scripting, text processing. Use scholar or sage avatar. Custom system prompt focused on Linux/scripting guidance without giving away lab answers.

findings.message: Aminos Bot — Cloud House Specialist (Cloud Architect)

meta.notes: Specialist bot for Cloud House. Train on AWS/Azure/cloud modules and cert prep content. Use architect avatar. Covers AWS CCP, Developer, Azure Fundamentals cert paths.

findings.message: Aminos Bot — Dark Arts Specialist (Cyber Hacker)

meta.notes: Specialist bot for Dark Arts House. Train on CTF concepts, security tools, pen testing methodology. Use hacker or pentester avatar. Must NOT reveal CTF flags or box solutions. Tight anti-jailbreak prompt — students WILL try.

findings.message: Aminos Bot — Signal House Specialist (Hardware Tinkerer)

meta.notes: Specialist bot for Signal House. Train on 20 Signal Toolkit tool pages, hardware platforms (RPi, Arduino, ESP32), IoT concepts. Use tinkerer or electrician avatar.

findings.message: Aminos Bot — Operator House Specialist (IT Ops Commander)

meta.notes: Specialist bot for Operator House. Train on IT operations, troubleshooting methodology, Dispatch scenarios, help desk concepts. Use commander or operator avatar.

findings.message: Aminos Bot — Code Armory Specialist (Code Debugger)

meta.notes: Specialist bot for Code Armory. Train on SQL modules, programming concepts, database fundamentals. Use debugger or ai-engineer avatar. Must not give direct SQL query answers for graded labs.

findings.message: Aminos Bot — Arctic House Specialist (Cert Scholar)

meta.notes: Specialist bot for Arctic House. Train on certification prep content, assessment strategies, study guides for CompTIA/AWS/Azure/Cisco certs. Use scholar or owl avatar. Must not leak exam answers.

findings.message: Container Sandbox — Docker Orchestration

meta.notes: Phase 2: Docker API, container lifecycle, idle timeout (30 min), resource limits (1 CPU, 512MB RAM, 2GB disk). Depends on Neon Server.

findings.message: Container Sandbox — WebSocket Terminal Relay

meta.notes: Phase 2: xterm.js frontend + WebSocket server on Neon. TLS encrypted. Reconnect on disconnect.

findings.message: Container Sandbox — 10 Per-Language Docker Images

meta.notes: Phase 2: armory-python, armory-c-cpp, armory-go, armory-rust, armory-assembly, armory-java, armory-csharp, armory-powershell, armory-php, armory-ruby.

findings.message: Container Sandbox — Security Isolation

meta.notes: Phase 2: Isolated Docker network, no host access, no outbound internet (or whitelisted repos), read-only base FS, writable /home/student only.

findings.message: Container Sandbox — Rate Limiting & Abuse Prevention

meta.notes: Phase 2: Max containers per user, creation cooldown, IP throttling, container count dashboard.

findings.message: Container Sandbox — Launch Sandbox UI

meta.notes: Phase 2: Launch button on track pages, loading spinner, session timer, reconnect handler.

findings.message: Container Sandbox — Full Capstone Image

meta.notes: Phase 2: armory-full image (~1.2GB) with all languages + nmap, wireshark-cli, metasploit-framework.

findings.message: Container Sandbox — Instructor Controls

meta.notes: Phase 2: Handler dashboard panel — active containers, force-kill, usage stats, per-student session history.

findings.message: Container Sandbox — Integration Testing

meta.notes: Phase 2: All 10 images verified, WebSocket reconnect, idle timeout, resource limits, security escape testing.

findings.message: Scraper Core — Forge Redesign for Resistant Targets

meta.notes: Redesign scraper-forge pipeline for 5 resistant targets that cannot discover pages: owasp, cisa-alerts, python-docs, aws-docs, azure-docs. Current Gemini-powered auto-healer keeps failing on these. Investigate root causes (anti-scraping protections, dynamic rendering, API gating). Evaluate alternative strategies: official APIs (OWASP wiki API, CISA KEV JSON feed, Python docs inventory), headless browser scraping (Playwright/Puppeteer), sitemap parsing, or manual URL seeding. Redesign forge template to handle these edge cases. Update targets.json with working configs.

findings.message: Eliminate lazy-loaded platform components — enforce static <script> tags + deliberate completion

meta.notes: HEUR-017 rule created to detect createElement('script') patterns loading platform components (ModuleProgress, GameTracker, etc.). Algorithm Chamber (30 files) already fixed — replaced 80% scroll auto-complete with deliberate 'Mark Complete' button. Scan any remaining lazy loaders across all houses and convert to static loads. The UX problem: auto-scroll completion fires before students finish reading and gives no feedback about what triggered it.

findings.message: Eliminate scroll-triggered auto-completion — convert 656 files to deliberate 'Mark Complete' buttons

meta.notes: HEUR-018 rule detects scroll-based completion (656 files). Breakdown: Code 210, AI 188, Web 163, Cloud 80, Shield 10, Key 3, Script 1, Eye 1. Algorithm Chamber challenges/capstone/geometry (30 files) already converted as proof-of-concept. Pattern: replace addEventListener('scroll') + ModuleProgress.complete() with a 'Mark Complete' button. Prioritize by student traffic — Code Armory and AI Cortex have the most files. Work house-by-house to avoid merge conflicts.

findings.message: House of the Matrix — Content Design & Build

meta.notes: Matrix house hub exists (index.html) with full scaffold: theme (#00ff41 green), mascot (Ghost), domain (Mechanics & Operations), cert badges (OSCP, GXPN, OSCE). Zero content — empty CATEGORIES, empty paths, 'Prestige Content Coming Soon' placeholder. Needs: (1) Define learning paths and categories aligned to OSCP/GXPN/OSCE objectives, (2) Design module structure — exploitation fundamentals, zero-day analysis, advanced pentesting, infrastructure operations, (3) Build initial module set with presentations, labs, quizzes, (4) Register in content-registry.js and ContentCatalog.js. The Matrix is the prestige house — content should be advanced-level, gated behind prerequisite houses (Dark Arts, Script, Key). Ghost as mascot sets the tone: covert, elite, infrastructure-focused.

findings.message: Add House of the Machine to the Sorting — make AI a sortable house

meta.notes: House of the Machine (ai) has 245 content files but is NOT in the sorting quiz. Students cannot be sorted into it. All other 10 content houses + Matrix are sortable. Needs: (1) Add 'ai' / 'machine' answer options to each sorting question in sorting.html, (2) Add .house-ai CSS theme color, (3) Add result container styling for Machine, (4) Verify dashboard handles 'ai' house assignment, (5) Test full sorting flow. The 12 sortable houses should be: Cloud, Code, Dark Arts, Eye, Forge, Key, Machine, Matrix, Script, Shield, Web, Divergent.

findings.message: Investigate prefers-reduced-motion across Hexworth — accessibility compliance for animations

meta.notes: External pentest flagged: animations (particle effects, typing, tagline decode, mascot loops, completion stamp slams) do not respect the prefers-reduced-motion OS setting. Users with vestibular disorders or motion sensitivity get the full animation experience with no opt-out. Investigation scope: (1) Audit which pages/components have animations — landing page particles, sorting page effects, mascot two-layer system, CompletionStamp/CLHCompletionModal, HouseRenderer, dashboard transitions, quiz feedback, (2) Determine the right behavior per component: disable entirely, reduce to fade-only, or show static state, (3) Implement via @media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) in CSS and matchMedia check in JS for requestAnimationFrame loops, (4) Consider a platform-wide animation toggle in user profile (persisted to localStorage) as a Hexworth-specific override independent of OS setting, (5) Check if this is required for WCAG 2.1 AA compliance (Section 508 / university requirements). The CSS fix is simple per-file but the JS animation loops (particles, typing, mascot) need matchMedia guards. Could also create an EduScan rule to detect requestAnimationFrame or setInterval animation loops without a prefers-reduced-motion check.

findings.message: House of the Divergent — Content Design & Build

meta.notes: Divergent = cross-domain polymath. Flux (Chimera) shifts between all houses because Divergent students connect domains rather than specialize. Has full branding (emblem, mascot, badges, hero animation) and 4 project files in _app/projects/ but NO house directory, NO hub page, NO curriculum. Curriculum direction: (1) Cross-domain capstone challenges — multi-house problems requiring Code + Security + Network + Cloud skills together, (2) Emerging tech — quantum computing, blockchain, IoT security, space systems — topics that don't fit one house, (3) Interdisciplinary labs — 'Build a secure CI/CD pipeline that deploys to K8s, monitors with SIEM, passes a pentest', (4) Career paths — CTO, architect, consultant tracks requiring breadth over depth, (5) The 4 existing projects (field-terminal, multi-tool, manim, discord-bot) become seed content. Build: (a) Create houses/divergent/ directory + hub page, (b) Define cross-domain paths and categories, (c) Migrate _app/projects/ into the house, (d) Cert alignment: CISSP, TOGAF, AWS Solutions Architect. Color: #ff00ff (magenta). Domain: 'Cross-Domain Mastery'.

findings.message: Scraper-core framework build — generalized multi-source scraping infrastructure

meta.notes: MARATHON ITEM (scraper-core). Full architecture in _tools/scraper-core/PLAN.md. SC-1 (framework), SC-2 (storage schema), SC-3 (MS Learn crawler), SC-4 (AI cert sweep), SC-5 (classifier), SC-6 (security sweep), SC-7 (Azure sweep), SC-8 (GitHub discovery). Python-based, shared caching, rate limiting, CLI, incremental scraping, content-hash dedup. Currently plan-only, no code. The working prototypes (ai-scraper + repo-scout + content-classifier) handle immediate needs. This sprint generalizes them into a production framework. Build when marathon time allows — not blocking any house content since prototypes work today.

findings.message: Ducky Course QC — completeness audit and fix all 8 modules

meta.notes: Honest QC of the 8-module DuckyScript course (ducky-course-01 through 08). Issues found: (1) Module 01: no verification after CircuitPython flash, hardcoded version number, no mention of where to save payload.dd, no troubleshooting, no testing walkthrough, no hardware photos/diagrams. (2) All modules: no lab environment setup instruction — students need a Windows VM as a safe target but this is never mentioned. (3) Modules 02-08: presentation-style with syntax examples but no hands-on exercises tied to the actual Pico hardware. Students learn DuckyScript in theory but never verify their payloads execute correctly. (4) No progressive build — modules don't reference previous module output or prepare for the next. (5) No troubleshooting sections for common failures (CIRCUITPY not mounting, payload not executing, antivirus blocking, wrong key mappings for non-US keyboards). (6) No connection to C2 dashboard LIVE mode — the ducky course should culminate in deploying payloads via C2. Fix approach: read each module as a complete beginner, add verification steps after every action, add troubleshooting callouts, add VM setup instructions in module 01, add hands-on exercises that require the physical Pico.

findings.message: Signal hardware project completeness audit — can each guide be followed start to finish?

meta.notes: Systematic QC of all Signal hardware projects (sg-01 through sg-92 plus ducky course). For EACH guide, answer: (1) Is the parts list complete and buyable? (2) Are download links current and working? (3) Does every command work if copy-pasted? (4) Is there a verification step after every action? (5) Are common failure modes documented with troubleshooting? (6) Can a beginner follow it with no prior experience beyond prerequisites? (7) Do wiring diagrams match the code pin assignments? (8) Is the progression from prerequisite projects smooth? Priority order: (a) Home Lab Builds sg-43 to sg-52 (new, need first pass), (b) Foundations sg-01 to sg-05 (existing, need freshness check), (c) Red Team HW / Ducky course (QC-34), (d) Remaining sections. Create an EduScan rule (SIGNAL-001) that checks for missing verification sections, missing troubleshooting callouts, and broken external URLs in Signal guides.

findings.message: CLH course consolidation — merge flat clh/ and courses/clh/modules/ into one canonical path

meta.notes: Two parallel file sets for CLH course: (1) flat clh/ directory with .applet.html/.lab.html/.quiz.html (31 chapters, old format, linked from ArcticData, content-registry, ContentCatalog), (2) courses/clh/modules/ with .module.html/.lab.html/.quiz.html (31 chapters, new format with richer content). Both are live, both reachable by students, quizzes share moduleIds but have different questions. CLH-016 through CLH-030 flat applets were missing Complete buttons (now fixed). Content may be additive — courses versions may have content the flat versions lack and vice versa. Merge plan: (1) For each chapter, compare flat vs courses content, keep the richer version, (2) Consolidate to one canonical path (courses/clh/modules/), (3) Update ArcticData.js, content-registry.js, ContentCatalog.js, CLHConfig.js to point to canonical path, (4) Redirect or remove flat files, (5) Verify quiz answer keys match the canonical version. The System Monitor project has checkpoint verification blocks (cyan callouts after each phase with specific test commands and expected output). The other 99 projects need the same treatment — 5 phases each = ~495 checkpoints to write. Each checkpoint tells the student exactly what to run and what to expect to verify they completed the phase correctly. Approach: read each phase description, determine the testable output, write 2-3 verification lines. Format: phase-checkpoint div with phase-checkpoint-label and phase-checkpoint-text. Can be done autonomously in marathon mode — no design decisions, just read phase + write test.

findings.message: Scrape content for Matrix + Divergent using existing prototype scrapers

meta.notes: MARATHON ITEM. Use working prototypes (ai-scraper + repo-scout + content-classifier) to scrape seed content for both new houses. No new scraper architecture needed — just new targets. MATRIX targets: (1) MS Learn: RHCSA paths, AZ-104 infra admin, Kubernetes learning paths, (2) GitHub: kubernetes-admin, ansible-enterprise, vmware-automation, prometheus-grafana repos, (3) Red Hat docs: systemd, SELinux, networking, (4) Kubernetes docs: CKA objectives, cluster admin. DIVERGENT targets: (1) MS Learn: CISSP-aligned paths, AWS SA paths, cross-domain architecture, (2) GitHub: full-stack-security, devsecops, iot-security, quantum-computing repos, (3) NIST: CSF, 800-53, RMF frameworks. Run on bc1 (100.96.136.114). Update content-classifier.js house mappings to recognize matrix and divergent. Output to shared Samba storage for review before importing to _app/houses/.

findings.message: Device Profile System — IDE and C2 multi-device support architecture

meta.notes: Design device profile system. Each supported device gets a profile with: name, chip, supported commands, deployment protocol, connection method. IDE shows commands per profile. C2 registers by profile type. Foundation for all HW items.

findings.message: USB Army Knife Integration — extended DuckyScript commands and WiFi deploy

meta.notes: Integrate USB Army Knife (ESP32-S3) into IDE. Extended commands: STORAGE, WIFI, MARAUDER, SCREEN, MIC. Syntax highlighting for extended set. Deploy via WiFi Bootstrap web interface. Field Manual with USB Army Knife docs. Ref: github.com/i-am-shodan/USBArmyKnife

findings.message: Pico-Ducky Integration — CircuitPython HID payload deployment

meta.notes: Raspberry Pi Pico with CircuitPython adafruit_hid. IDE exports as code.py for drag-and-drop or WiFi deploy via Pico W. Most accessible device at 4 dollars.

findings.message: ESP32 Device Agent — heartbeat, telemetry, and command polling firmware

meta.notes: Reference firmware for ESP32 devices that registers with Hexworth C2, sends heartbeat and sensor telemetry, polls for commands, and reports results. Written in Arduino/PlatformIO. Connects to C2 Cloud Functions (c2Register, c2CheckIn, c2GetCommands, c2Result). Students flash this to their ESP32 and see it appear on the C2 dashboard.

findings.message: Raspberry Pi Agent — Python-based C2 agent for Linux devices

meta.notes: Python agent script for Raspberry Pi that registers with C2, reports system info (CPU, memory, network, uptime), polls for commands, executes safely sandboxed tasks, and reports results. Pairs with Signal House home lab projects (SG-43 through SG-52).

findings.message: Flipper Zero Integration — BadUSB and SubGHz command support

meta.notes: Add Flipper Zero as a device profile. IDE exports payloads in Flipper BadUSB format (.txt with Flipper-specific syntax). Document SubGHz, RFID, NFC, and IR capabilities in the Field Manual. No direct WiFi deploy (Flipper uses SD card).

findings.message: Digispark and CJMCU Integration — ATtiny85 and ATmega32U4 targets

meta.notes: Add Digispark (ATtiny85) and CJMCU BadUSB (ATmega32U4) as device profiles. IDE exports as Arduino sketches. These are the cheapest HID devices (2-5 dollars). Limited command set — basic DuckyScript only, no WiFi.

findings.message: Signal House Hardware Lab Guide — USB Army Knife build project

meta.notes: New Signal House project guide: Build and Flash USB Army Knife. Students purchase LilyGo T-Dongle S3 (8-15 dollars), flash USB Army Knife firmware via PlatformIO, configure WiFi, connect to Hexworth C2, and write their first payload in the DuckyScript IDE. Ties IDE, C2, and hardware together.

findings.message: C2 Dashboard Device Detail Panels — per-device type UI

meta.notes: Enhance C2 dashboard with device-type-specific detail panels. ESP32 shows: WiFi signal, firmware version, flash size, sensor readings. Raspberry Pi shows: CPU, memory, disk, network, running services. USB Army Knife shows: attack status, payload queue, WiFi clients. Each device type gets a tailored view.

findings.message: End-to-End Hardware Lab Test — verify full IDE to C2 to device pipeline

meta.notes: Full integration test: Student writes DuckyScript in IDE, deploys to USB Army Knife via WiFi, device executes payload, results appear in C2 dashboard. Verify the complete loop works end-to-end with real hardware. Document the test procedure for QC.

findings.message: HEX-Board Student View — locked class dashboard

findings.message: HEX-Board Instructor Panel — admin console integration

findings.message: Syllabus Builder — drag content into ordered assignments

findings.message: Content Lockdown Middleware — restrict student navigation

meta.notes: HEX-Board students cannot browse outside their assigned content. Any navigation attempt redirects to HEX-Board. Uses tenant config to whitelist allowed URLs.

findings.message: Sequential Unlock Logic — configurable prerequisite chains

meta.notes: Assignment N+1 locked until N complete. Configurable: strict sequence, open access, or custom prerequisites. Visual lock indicators in student view.

findings.message: Due Date Engine — deadlines, overdue flagging, late policy

meta.notes: Assignments have due dates. Overdue items flagged red in student view and gradebook. Configurable late policy (accept late, penalty, hard cutoff).

findings.message: Gradebook Component — student x assignment score matrix

meta.notes: All students x all assignments. Color-coded cells (green/yellow/red). Sortable by student or assignment. Click cell for detail. The heart of the instructor experience.

findings.message: Engagement Analytics Dashboard — hotspots and dropout detection

meta.notes: Per-module: time spent, completion rate, dropout point, quiz pass rate, average score. Heatmap view. Identifies where students get stuck.

findings.message: Grade Export — CSV with scores, times, attempts

meta.notes: Export gradebook as CSV. Columns: student name, email, assignment title, score, percentage, completion date, attempts, time spent. Compatible with institutional grade import.

findings.message: CTF Tournament as Graded Assignment — wire into gradebook

meta.notes: Instructor assigns a CTF tournament as a graded event. Tournament scores flow into the gradebook. Team scores can map to individual grades.

meta.notes: Instructor posts announcements visible on HEX-Board student view. Supports pinning, timestamps, read tracking. Uses existing messaging infrastructure.
